summary: This UC Master Gardener page explains soluble salt buildup in house plant soil, which comes from dissolved minerals and fertilizer left behind as water evaporates. It describes the symptoms and how salts damage roots, and gives prevention methods, mainly proper drainage and periodic leaching. It also notes that salt tolerance varies by species and growing conditions.
one_line: Guide to recognizing, preventing, and fixing soluble salt buildup in house plant soil through drainage, leaching, and repotting.
key_facts: Soluble salts may accumulate on top of the soil as a yellow or white crust, or as a ring around the pot at the soil line or drainage hole.
Salts may also build up on the outside of clay pots.
Signs of excess soluble salts in house plants include reduced growth, brown leaf tips, dropping of lower leaves, small new growth, dead root tips, and wilting.
Soluble salts are minerals dissolved in water; fertilizer dissolved in water becomes a soluble salt.
When water evaporates from soil, the minerals or salts stay behind, and rising concentration makes it harder for plants to take up water.
At extremely high salt levels, water can be pulled out of the root tips, causing them to die.
High salt levels damage roots directly and make plants more susceptible to insects and diseases; root rot is one of the most common associated problems.
To prevent injury, let some water drain through the container and empty the saucer; do not let the pot sit in water, or the washed-out salts are reabsorbed.
House plants should be leached at least every 4 to 6 months.
To leach a plant, pour water through the soil and let it drain completely, using an amount equal to twice the volume of the pot.
If a salt crust has formed, remove it before leaching, taking no more than 1/4 inch (6 mm) of soil, and preferably do not add soil to the top of the pot.
If the soluble salt level appears extremely high, repot the plant.
Salt tolerance varies by species and how the plant is grown; a greenhouse plant with well-managed watering may tolerate high salt levels that would injure a house plant.
Some nurseries and retail outlets leach plants before sale; if unsure whether a new plant was leached, leach it the first time you water.
